source.title: TuringViT: Making SOTA Vision Transformers Accessible to All
source.authors: Qiman Wu; Hanlin Chen; Lyujie Chen; Rui Xin; Jianlei Zheng; Mingyuan Wang; Jiahui Hu; Da Zhu; Yuecheng Ma; Yuhua Wei; Yizhao Wang; Hua Zhou; Yuheng Zhang; Anhua Liu; Shaman Tang; Yue He; Pengfei Diao; Shuang Su; Haotong Xin; Weichao Huang; Hang Zhang; Xianming Liu

record.file_problem: none; the full technical report is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether downstream performance changes predictably with data scale, using zero-shot vision benchmarks rather than language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The data-scaling study reports zero-shot classification performance for TuringViT-18L as image-text training data increases from 20M to 850M pairs. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, parameter- or compute-scaling laws, compute-optimal allocation, or extrapolation from small runs. Figure 7 gives the scaling results as plots; no point values are stated in the text. Other benchmark comparisons and the VLM evaluations do not test the versions recorded here.
record.test_reason: A controlled data-scaling sweep (TuringViT-18L, 20M/100M/850M image-text pairs, same recipe, 10 epochs) reports how downstream zero-shot accuracy changes with data scale. This is a new setting (a contrastive vision encoder) for V6, downstream predictability with scale. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1, V2, V3, V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right for the scaling section: zero-shot accuracy improves systematically with curated data from 20M to 850M pairs, described as a power law with no saturation. The report's main conclusion is broader. TuringViT matches or beats open ViT baselines such as SigLIP2 with about 10% of their data, and has better high-resolution latency scaling.
record.recipe_differences: This is a visual contrastive-pretraining data-scale sweep with zero-shot classification outcomes, not language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The report says gains are especially pronounced on ObjectNet and ImageNet-A compared with the other evaluated benchmarks.
record.problems: Figure 7 is the only reported result for the scaling sweep, and its point values are not stated in the text. The report gives no fitted exponent or fitting details, and the sweep covers only one model variant and data scales up to 850M pairs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional data-scaling result rows left out. Other results in Sections 3.1–3.4 do not test the versions recorded here.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported for any scaling axis.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison. The 18L and 24L variants differ in depth and in parameter count.
Pretraining loss scaling in the vision setting is not reported. Only downstream accuracy is.

Language-model downstream tasks are not tested. Parameter or compute scaling is not tested in a controlled way. Prediction from pretraining loss is not tested. Extrapolation of the downstream fit to larger scale is not tested. No fitted curve or exponent is reported.
No comparison of fitting choices, and no test of whether the curve bends.

missing.what: Model-size comparison at fixed data (0.85B pairs): TuringViT-18L vs 24L average zero-shot accuracy, 82.7 vs 83.6. Parameter counts are not stated. Only two points, and depth is confounded with size.

record.verdict_notes: The 'power law' description rests on three data points shown only in Figure 7, with no exponent or fit reported. Linking these rows to V6 assumes V6 extends beyond language models to vision encoders. A stricter reading would treat this as a V5/V6 cross-modal downstream result. Data and compute co-vary because epochs are fixed, and model size is fixed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and its trend with compute.
The effect of architecture details on loss at a fixed parameter count.
The claimed loss-scaling law in other modalities or training regimes; this study measures zero-shot classification performance, not pretraining loss.
The study varies image-text data volume for one visual model; it does not test language-model downstream performance, model-size scaling, or predictability from pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and whether curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: TuringViT-18L contrastive vision encoder, six zero-shot classification benchmarks, data scaled 20M→850M pairs at a fixed 10 epochs
relationships.reason: The text says accuracy rises consistently and 'gains follow a power law' with no saturation (R1–R6). The evidence is weak: three points, figure-only values, and no fitted parameters.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increases consistently across three data scales, with gains described as following a power law without saturation, although fitted parameters are unavailable.
